notes: Panel scenarios: a slash command that opens a panel or picker belongs here, and the assertions are about what the surface renders and how it is dismissed. Anything asserting a domain effect the panel merely reports -- what is attached to context, which agent is live, which session resumed -- lives with its domain instead. Panels are live regions that are erased on dismissal rather than committed to scrollback, so a string only asserts what is on screen at the moment verify runs; the strings gated by waitForText steps are the ones that must have rendered at some point. Turns are inline per scenario, and panel-opening scenarios need a sticky catch-all because opening one makes backend bookkeeping calls beyond any scripted prompt.

scenarios.name: Bare /context opens the panel collapsed
scenarios.description: Bare /context is the glance form and must stay collapsed, while /context show is the detail form -- a regression that flipped the default would bury the summary under a file list or hide the list from the user who asked for it
scenarios.observe: The summary and the expand affordance render while the detail section does not. The file is attached first on purpose: it makes the negatives a statement about the collapsed default hiding detail that exists, rather than about an empty panel. The footer hint is the discriminator -- it reads 'to expand' only in the collapsed state and 'to collapse' only in the expanded one, so the two forms of the command cannot both satisfy this.

scenarios.name: Agent picker lists the registry with the active agent marked
scenarios.description: The picker must show real registry entries and mark which one is live, so a user can see what they are choosing between
scenarios.observe: The source group cell and the active marker are both produced per row from the registry the backend advertised, so neither can render from an empty list -- which is what separates this from asserting the picker chrome alone. The empty-state negative pins that the word 'agent' on screen came from a populated picker rather than the no-agents alert.

scenarios.name: Session picker lists sessions and hands the prompt back on escape
scenarios.description: The /sessions picker takes over the whole screen, so it must list the current session and give the prompt back when dismissed -- a picker that cannot be escaped strands the user
scenarios.observe: The picker renders its column header and search placeholder, then escape returns to the prompt. Those two picker strings are gated by waitForText steps rather than verify on purpose: the picker is a full-screen takeover whose content never enters scrollback, so it is absent from the settled frame once dismissed -- the waitForText step catches them while the picker is still up, and fails if they never render. Verify then carries the other half: the prompt placeholder is off screen entirely while the picker is up, so finding it proves the takeover was dismissed rather than merely opened.

scenarios.name: Typing in the dashboard search narrows to matching sessions
scenarios.description: The dashboard's search field is how a user finds one conversation among many, so typing must filter the rows rather than only decorate the field
scenarios.observe: Two sessions exist with distinct titles, and typing part of one leaves only that row. The excluded title is the discriminating half: a field that accepted the text without filtering would keep both rows, and both titles were on screen before the query was typed. Titles are derived from each session's first prompt, so neither string is anything the scenario typed into the dashboard.

scenarios.name: The /tools panel lists the tool groups
scenarios.description: User opens the /tools panel to review the tool permission configuration; the panel lists the builtin tool groups (read, shell, web, write) with a filter — the tool-trust management surface
scenarios.observe: The /tools slash command opens the panel listing the builtin tool groups with a search filter and an esc-to-close hint. What is pinned is that the list rendered and was populated from the tool registry -- two distinct group names cannot come from chrome. What is NOT pinned is any trust state, filtering behaviour, or per-tool permission, despite this being the trust-management surface; the permissions category covers the trust verbs separately.

scenarios.name: An agent's hooks are listed with the trigger and command they will run
scenarios.description: Two hooks declared by the planted agent, on different triggers -- asserts the listing names each one's resolved trigger and the exact command, and counts them
scenarios.observe: The command strings are asserted verbatim because they are what will actually run: a listing that named the hook but not its command would leave a user unable to tell which of several hooks is about to execute. The run waits on one hook's command and asserts the other's, so neither is a restatement of the other, and the count is left as a predicate that fails if the panel finds more or fewer hooks than were declared. Both triggers are asserted because the config spells one `agentSpawn` while the row reads SessionStart, so the pair proves the vocabulary is resolved rather than echoed.

scenarios.name: With no hooks declared the listing says so instead of rendering an empty table
scenarios.description: An agent declaring no hooks -- asserts the listing reports zero and states the absence, rather than showing headers over no rows
scenarios.observe: The empty state is the counterpart to the populated listing: the same panel and the same chrome, distinguished by the count and the stated absence. It runs against the default agent, which declares no hooks, rather than a planted agent with its hooks removed -- so what it pins is that an agent without hooks reports none, not that removing hooks from one agent empties the list. Both trigger names are asserted absent because they are what appears once any hook is read, so a panel that listed hooks from somewhere other than the active agent would fail here rather than looking merely empty.

scenarios.name: The model picker lists every model the registry offers and marks the active one
scenarios.description: The model picker opened on a three-model registry -- asserts each entry appears with the description the registry supplied, the active model is marked, and the list is navigable
verify: screen.contains:Served by mock-krs-server so a prompt can reach the fake KRS.
screen.contains:Second registry entry, advertising an effort ladder.
screen.contains:Third registry entry, advertising no effort ladder.
scenarios.observe: Every entry is asserted by the description the registry supplied rather than by its model name, because the names are also rendered elsewhere -- the active one sits in the status line -- while the descriptions exist nowhere but the rows. Asserting all three is what proves the list is the registry's rather than a truncation of it. The credits column is not asserted: the fixture serves no rate data, so every row shows the '----- credits' placeholder, which would pass regardless of the list being right. The navigate hint only appears once there is more than one row, so it fails on a picker that collapsed the registry to a single entry.

scenarios.name: A model that advertises effort levels offers them and marks the one in force
scenarios.description: The effort picker opened on a model whose registry entry declares an effort enum -- asserts every advertised level is offered, the level in force is marked, and the status line carries it
steps: waitForText:Switched to Mock KRS Effort Model
scenarios.observe: The three levels are the enum the registry advertised, so asserting all of them proves the ladder was read from the model rather than being a fixed list the client carries. The marked level is asserted as one needle with its marker, which pins the mark onto the level the schema names as its default -- the level in force before anything is chosen, and a ladder offered with nothing marked would leave a user unable to tell what they are already running. What the level does once chosen is a domain effect and is asserted with the model journeys, not here. The navigate hint only appears once there is more than one row, so it fails on a ladder collapsed to a single level.

scenarios.name: The effort picker distinguishes the level in force from the model's own default
scenarios.description: The effort picker reopened after a non-default level was chosen -- asserts the chosen level is marked as in force, the model's advertised default is marked as the default, and the old marking is gone
steps: waitForText:Switched to Mock KRS Effort Model
scenarios.observe: Two different facts share one column: which level is in force, and which one the model advertises as its default. Until a level is chosen they are the same row and the picker cannot be shown to tell them apart, which is why this reopens the picker after choosing the level that is not the default. Each marker is asserted as one needle with its level, so a picker that put the right markers on the wrong rows fails; the negative names the row that was marked in force before the choice, which is what a stale marker would leave behind. The needles carry the column spacing, so if the widths change they fail together and loudly rather than one silently matching elsewhere.

scenarios.name: The help panel lists the commands with their descriptions and subcommands
scenarios.description: The help panel opened on the full command catalogue -- asserts commands are listed with the descriptions the registry supplies, that a command carrying subcommands names them, and that the panel says how to scroll and close
scenarios.observe: Help is where a user goes when they do not know what exists, so a listing that rendered its chrome and none of its rows would be the worst kind of pass. Each command is asserted by the description the registry supplies rather than by its name, because the names are also what the run types and what the slash menu shows, while the descriptions exist nowhere but these rows. The subcommand line is asserted for a command that has them, since a catalogue that silently flattened them would leave every subcommand undiscoverable. The scroll hint is asserted because the catalogue is longer than the window and a user who cannot tell it scrolls sees a truncated list as the whole truth.

scenarios.name: The config panel lists every configuration category with its source and status
scenarios.description: The config panel opened on a workspace with some categories populated and some empty -- asserts the table names each category, reports where it came from, and marks an unconfigured one as absent rather than omitting the row
steps: waitForText:Cloud configs apply to cloud sessions
scenarios.observe: This panel answers "what is configured, and where did it come from?", so the load-bearing row is the empty one: MCP servers are asserted present with the dash that marks them unconfigured, because dropping a category a user has not set up is what makes the panel useless for working out why something is missing. The column header is asserted with its spacing so the three facts stay distinguishable -- a table that lost the Source column would still contain every category name. The populated categories are asserted by name only, deliberately: their counts come from whatever the workspace happens to hold and would make this journey fail on an unrelated file being added.

scenarios.name: The changelog panel opens scrollable and escape returns to the prompt
scenarios.description: The changelog panel opened and then dismissed -- asserts the release notes render as a scrollable overlay and that escape removes it and gives the prompt back, rather than leaving the panel or a blank region behind
verify: screen.contains:ask a question or describe a task
scenarios.observe: Opening and dismissing is the whole contract for a read-only overlay, and the dismissal is the half that breaks: a panel left on screen, or torn down leaving a blank region where the prompt should be, is the failure a user cannot work around. The two waits carry the positive half -- the panel appeared under its own title and reported itself scrollable -- so the predicates are free to assert the state after escape, where both strings must be gone and the prompt back. The notes themselves are not asserted: their content is whatever the release carried, so pinning any entry would make this journey fail on the next release rather than on a regression.
